#5462. FHFA Increases Conforming Loan Limit by $22k for 2027

The Federal Housing and Finance Authority (FHFA) has announced a new conforming loan limit (the maximum dollar amount for a conventional mortgage) for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages in 2027. The new limit for one-unit properties will be $855,400, up $22,650 from 2026’s limit.

The Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) requires FHFA to adjust the Enterprises’ baseline conforming loan limit each year to reflect the change in the average U.S. home price, according to a release. As the organization’s research found that home prices were up 2.72% on average from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026, the FHFA said that the conforming loan limit has increased on the same baseline.

In addition, high cost areas (where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline conforming loan limit) have a higher limit due to HERA, according to a release. The high cost area limit sits at a ceiling of 150% the baseline limit, which in 2027 will be $1,283,100.

The FHFA also noted special statutory provisions establishing different loan limits for Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the baseline loan limit and the ceiling loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100 and $1,924,650, respectively.

Due to rising home values, the FHFA stated that the conforming loan limit will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their new home in the Cotswalds, and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood, the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom.

Northwood shared a look inside the family's latest digs in a Nov. 22 Instagram post, noting that he and Markle had recently spent quite a bit of quality time together, including a lunch date and a visit to her new property.

During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood said they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah, "who has just started weaning" and is exploring new foods.

"She was very excited for all the new flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment."

Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a New York-inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website, Northwood divulged more about their catchup.

"I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood said of their lunch date. "Since we last saw each other, she’s had her second baby and I’ve had my first. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world."

Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything."

The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet.

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail.

They first made plans to establish a private residence in the U.K. in August of this year, six years after quitting their roles as working members of the British royal family to relocate to a $14.7 million home in Montecito, CA.

Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false."

In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family."

"Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me," he said of Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. "I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience."

He also admitted that "it's nice to be back" on "U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there."

The family plans to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas.

During a Nov. 20 appearance on the British morning show, "This Morning," Harry revealed the family's plans for Thanksgiving and Christmas, noting that mother-in-law Doria Ragland will be joining them.

"My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he said, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu.

The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography.

"Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People. "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.

"Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone," the source added.

#5460. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5456. Infamous ‘Hoarders’ Mansion in North Carolina Sells for $3.85 Million After Jaw-Dropping Restoration

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by New York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

After 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

“They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”

In addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it says ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

After the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

“Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you plan your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

The property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only showed it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” said Chesnutt.

After over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The new owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” said Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”

Chesnutt could not disclose whether the the new owners plan to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

“It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” said Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”

#5453. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5452. Attached Homes Drive Salt Lake City’s New-Home Sales Growth

New home demand in Salt Lake City is increasingly splitting along product lines, with attached housing gaining momentum while detached sales remain comparatively flat.

In September, annualized new-home sales across the metro topped 2,800 units, up roughly 4% from a year ago. Attached housing drove much of the gain, with annualized sales reaching 1,350 units, a 10% increase year over year. Meanwhile, detached sales remained slightly higher at 1,450 units but edged down 0.7% from last year.

Although detached homes still accounted for more sales in absolute terms, virtually all of the market’s recent growth stemmed from attached product. Active project counts showed a similar pattern. As of November, Salt Lake City had 92 active detached new-home projects, down 3.2%, compared with 65 attached projects, up 3.2%.

Pricing helps explain why attached housing may be resonating with buyers, especially given today’s affordability challenges. As of July, the average list price for a new detached home was roughly $738,000, up 11% from a year earlier, while new attached homes averaged approximately $470,000, up about 4%. That puts the difference between the two averages at more than $268,000, although it is important to note that attached and detached homes differ in size, location, design, and community mix.

The distribution of closings reinforces that distinction. In the past 12 months ending August, attached new-home closings were concentrated heavily in lower price bands, particularly between $350,000 and $450,000. Detached closings were distributed much more broadly, with the most substantial shares falling between $450,000 and $650,000.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

#5449. Judge Upholds Mamdani’s NYC Rent Freeze, Tosses Landlords’ Lawsuit

A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.

In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, New York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.

Despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision.

The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote, with only Arpit Gupta, an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams, voting no.

But it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze.

Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes.

Operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially.

“Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in June.

Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid."

The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal.

#5444. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”

#5443. What Next-Gen Real Estate Leaders Are Leaving Behind and Embracing Instead

Above, from left, Eric Fite, Jack Markham, Marisela Harper, Lori Muller and Adrian Provost

“All the technology in the world doesn’t matter unless it makes a fundamental impact on the relationship with the client, the way we serve them. That’s our true north.”

That was the sentiment summed up by Eric Fite, COO of CENTURY 21 Judge Fite Company in Dallas/Fort Worth, when moderating a recent panel of up-and-coming brokerage leaders about what old ways they are leaving behind and what innovative new approaches they are bringing to the fore.

AI and technology and how they can best be used dominated the discussion, but panelists also shared some of the ways they are reimagining traditional business practices to support their agents in the session titled, “Next-Gen Leaders and Their Powerful New Approach to Business,” held this past October at RISMedia’s CEO Exchange in Washington, D.C.

In addition to Fite, the panel included Marisela Harper, broker/owner of ClearView Realty; Adrian Provost, CEO of ONE Terminus & LEVEL; Lori Muller, president of Fathom Realty; and Jack Markham, chief marketing officer at Inside Real Estate.

The group also shared insights into how they are positioning their tech stacks and CRMs, how they are viewing their data and data ownership and control,as well as the future of AI and how it can assist agents through automation.

“I think everybody’s realizing that the CRM is not necessarily your tech stack,” said Markham when asked what old beliefs most forward-thinking brokerages have already abandoned. “Traditionally, you would pick a CRM, and that’s where your data is; that’s who owns the workflows. But quite honestly, the smartest brokers are realizing that the tech stack is way more than your CRM.

“Most teams are running two to three CRMs. And that’s not because everybody loves using multiple CRMs. They do it because it’s a fear of loss. They do it because if I drop a tech stack, if I drop a tool, I don’t want to lose my data. And so they’re doing it as insurance. So I think most of the smart brokers today are realizing they don’t need more tools in the tech stack. They don’t need another tool, another app. What they need is something to absorb the tech stack, something that’s going to empower their data so their agents think less about where they log in and more about how to drive conversations.”

Provost said he views the “tech stack,” or the set of software tools, apps and technologies a company uses, as more of a folder, and a platform as more of an operating system.

“Ultimately, what I look for is how (tech) helps close certain loops that lead to that appointment-to-close loop, and then to that close-to-repeat-and-referral-business. I think that if it’s something that isn’t touching one of those or enhancing the agent’s ability to perform, then it probably doesn’t really belong in the tech or in the platform.”

Fite then turned the conversation to AI, asking panelists how they are using it and consumer behavior data to identify when and how an agent should engage a consumer.

“With consumer behavior data, that data is your opportunity,” Muller said. “It’s your opportunity to be strategic with what you’re going to do with it, how you’re going to utilize it. And then AI is the actual action step. It’s how you take action with that data to create a result.”

Markham said it’s all about control over data.

“The uncomfortable question for most brokers is, if you decided to leave your tools or your tech stack, could you take your data with you? And the answer most likely for most brokers in the industry is no,” he said. “They find out far too late that they can’t take it with them. Real ownership of data means you control that data no matter what CRM or tech tool you’re using.”

On a question about what work AI should be doing for a human, Provost said:

“I look at it from an operational standpoint. How can AI assist me and my agents in enhancing our service to our clients? And in my case, my clients being the agent. And so I think that humans need to always be in the loop. There should never be one point where they’re disconnected, but it should be streamlined, and we should be able to have AI connect components that don’t normally talk to one another so we can perform better and elevate that entire experience for whoever’s on the opposite end of it.”

Muller added that AI can help with automating transaction management, marketing solutions, social media, communication or “B- and C-level” operational tasks, while leaving more time for the most important aspect of the business—client relationships.

“No matter who tries to destroy the real estate industry, you can’t take the relational side away from the Realtor® and the consumer. AI is not going to do it. Technology’s not going to do it. That’s the most important thing we have to look at,” she said.

How does the next generation of real estate business leaders view traditional ways of supporting agents, or “loving on them,” as the panel discussed?

“We really do everything so strategically to love on the agent, down to when we built our office four years ago,” said Harper. “We built this big hub and we put our offices right where people that come in can see us. And that’s done on purpose. We have our staff completely trained to love on the agent. We also train our mentors to love on the agents. And when I say love, that’s really being intentionally present with them, spending the time to go to their weddings, go to the baby showers, attend the funerals because that’s a time when they really need just someone to be there for them.”

She added, “And one of the most important things on that contact card is the agent’s birthday. And that might seem so silly, but when I open my calendar for the day, I see whose birthday it is and that’s the first phone call I make just to call them and wish them a happy birthday. Of course, we do the birthday cards and the gift card and all of that, but the call just to wish them happy birthday, see how they’re doing, it goes over so well. They absolutely love it.”

Here are some more notable quotes from the session:

What’s most important when an agent leaves the brokerage?

Lori Muller: When an agent leaves, sometimes they leave because they think the grass is greener on the other side, and they get over there and it’s not. So I think it’s super important to have some type of exit strategy when an agent leaves and have a conversation to say, “Hey, what could we have done better? What was the situation that caused you to leave?” And it’s a teaching moment for both people. We also just recently did a comeback campaign where we called agents that have left over the last two years, and we have had almost a 25% return rate.

Are we heading toward a world where technology becomes table stakes and culture, service and execution become the real differentiators?

Jack Markham: I think you could take two people and give them the same tech stack, and what’s really going to separate them is not necessarily the tools that you’re using. It’s once you plug in your data, right? Once you plug in those relationships, once you plug in the trust, once you plug in the consumer behaviors that you’ve been tracking and the history behind that, it becomes your thumbprint. What’s unique and can’t be copied is all the history there. It’s all the relationships, it’s all the trust that becomes your thumbprint. And so that can never really be duplicated.

What’s the one move you would make over the next 12 months to better position your brokerage and your agents for where the industry is going?

Jack Markham: Figure out if you own your data. Meaning if you left today, some of your tools, could you take them with you? And if the answer is no, then I would fix that.

Marisela Harper: I would say just be super, super present because (agents) need that from you, and just show the love. And when I say show the love, I really mean truly say, “I love you.” Sometimes people might know that you love them, but they need to hear it too.

Lori Muller: Embrace your relationship with not only your technology, but your people. Longevity is in the relationship with the people; tech stack and your technology is constantly changing.

Adrian Provost: Move away from tech stacks completely and create platforms. The old days are completely over. Whatever you need, you can literally build it. And so I would move away from being so reliant on a tech stack and subscriptions and actually figure out what it is that your agents need and provide that to them.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5442. ‘Selling Sunset’ Alum Emma Hernan Reveals How Her West Hollywood Kitchen Launched Her Food Empire

Before she ever became a luxury real estate agent at The Oppenheim Group or appeared on the Netflix hit “Selling Sunset,” serial entrepreneur Emma Hernan had hired Jason Oppenheim to help her buy a home in West Hollywood, where she has since launched several successful businesses.

The 1940-built Colonial-style estate that Hernan bought in 2017 was a hot commodity, seeing as Oppenheim had initially hoped to snap up the property for himself, Hernan, 34, reveals to Realtor.com in the latest Celebrity Sanctuary.

“Funny enough, Jason really wanted to buy this house but he had just purchased another home, so he wanted someone that he at least knows to get it. I ended up buying it off market with Jason as my broker,” she explains.

Throughout the house hunt, Oppenheim encouraged Hernan to learn the real estate ropes so she could go from being his client to becoming his coworker and costar. After getting her real estate license in 2018, she “immediately hung [her] license with The O Group … and ended up on the show.”

Though Hernan left “Selling Sunset” in 2025 after six seasons as a main cast member, she still works with Oppenheim and other former costars—just without the added conflict that comes with filming reality TV.

“I would describe it in one word: Peaceful,” Hernan says about her experience in the office now that she’s not on the show.

However, Hernan still credits the series for giving her a platform to pursue other ventures alongside luxury real estate, such as her frozen seafood and empanada brand, Coast to Coast Kitchen, which officially debuted in 2025 but had been in the works for decades.

Hernan “grew up passing out crab cakes at demos and supermarkets” because her grandfather was the founder of the Massachusetts-based seafood company, Yankee Trader Seafood. When Hernan’s mother and aunt took over and needed capital to keep the enterprise going, Hernan lent them money she had earned from modeling, nannying, and investing in the stock market.

Beyond providing funding for equipment and employees, Hernan even bought a manufacturing facility in Hingham, MA that still services her family’s company as well as other food brands. She also owns a house in Norwell, MA next door to her brother’s abode, and is often in the area because of business and her boyfriend.

“Obviously, Boston is very special to me, but L.A.—I created Coast to Coast out of that kitchen with family,” she shares to illustrate why her West Coast residence holds a special place in her heart.

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Hernan points out the potential she’s always seen in the 3,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, four-bathroom, two-story dwelling she shares with her two dogs and eight rescue cats. Plus, she opens up about how the familiar New England feel of her home kitchen helps her feed every passion.

I purchased the home in 2017 for $2.7 million and … was renting it out. I had it as an investment property because it was a bit big for me by myself. When I started filming the show, my house is super conveniently located to the office, so I moved in right when I started filming.

This specific house and street, it's super conveniently located. It’s in the heart of West Hollywood. The office is right there. The location is a 10 for sure.

There's a lot of modern homes out there. I was looking for a while and didn't fall in love with anything. Then when I walked in here, it reminded me of New England and my family's home.

It was built in 1940. [The previous owners] did a small remodel [in] 1948 and then right before I purchased it, they did another small remodel, updated [the] kitchen and all that.

I redid the pool. The flooring is original and that's something that I go back and forth with changing, even though I do want to re-do the floors and warm them up. They're wood floors, original from 1940.

The house has so much potential, which is one of the reasons why I bought it. I didn't want to buy a house that was completely done. I wanted to be able to add value and make some money off of it. I actually just had a couple contractors come by and [give a] quote.

I'm definitely gonna do a pretty big remodel. It's very home-y, but it needs updates and I'm super excited to do that. I’m gonna do the full landscaping. It needs new floors, windows, all the things, but I think it'll be a really fun project.

I haven't really made it my own besides the kitchen, which I would say is my sanctuary: somewhere that feels safe, homey, and peaceful. That's really important. My life is very public and having that peace and a place that feels home-y and safe, that's definitely what [sanctuary] means to me.

“Selling Sunset” [was] different than [selling] real estate because [reality TV is] a little bit more drama heavy, so … a lot of times when I would come home from filming, cooking and creating meals for my friends and my family really did help separate that scene that we just had that was so crazy and so hectic. Coming home and forgetting all about that, chopping the vegetables that I was gonna serve for dinner, and really being able to separate the two—I did that all in the kitchen.

The kitchen, when I bought it, was definitely one of my favorite things about the whole house. It reminded me about New England and my family. I added some family photos. I’m from Scituate, MA. I added this cool little Scituate plaque.

It’s bright and white, but there's a lot of wood in there, too, which warms it up. Granite countertops, they're white. It's a very warm and bright kitchen. There's a lot of light that comes through. It really is my favorite part of the whole home.

The dining room area … I have a really beautiful [Restoration Hardware] dining room table that I love. And then I have this little countertop area.

I've created businesses there. I’ve closed deals there. I've had family gatherings there. I’ve had Thanksgiving there, Christmas there, and so many fun little taco nights with my friends that now became my family. I’ve gone on QVC live from the kitchen. I have been in glam for “Selling Sunset.” So many of my interviews—everything's from my kitchen. It’s really special to me.

The stove was literally where I created half of my recipes for Coast to Coast. So many meals are created in there. I love to cook. It's such a passion of mine. It’s therapeutic for me and that's why I was like, “I need to start my own company.

I'm gonna get a new oven, a new SubZero, and all of that. The one thing that it's lacking is storage. I had this open space area where there's glasses, but there's not enough cabinetry, especially for the amount of cooking that I do.

I definitely tend to overcook because I'd rather have more than enough food than not enough. I love to cook and have many options for people. It's funny because my mom and my dad are like, “Do you need help? What do you need help with?” And I really don't need help. I love doing it. I love making every dish, making it special. I love plating it and making it look really good.

Presentation is key. I love it on a white plate, all decorative. I like everything to match. I love it to look nice, even when I'm setting up the table with nice placemats and making the table look really nice.

Some of the stuff is antique. All of my stuff in Boston was my grandmother's that was passed down. Then I've just gotten a lot of the white, classic, Crate and Barrel stuff for the L.A. [kitchen] because I'm not going to ship my really nice stuff over to L.A., especially our sentimental family pieces.

All of my guests, as soon as somebody walks in, I'm like, “What can I make you?” It doesn't matter if they're stopping over for 10 minutes. I have friends that will pop over and I’ll be like, “Do you want me to make you a sandwich? Do you want me to make you a quesadilla or throw in my empanadas?” Making people feel at home makes a difference.

What's really special about the two industries that I'm in that I genuinely love so much—it doesn't feel like work to me. I'm super grateful and I thoroughly enjoy both.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. Karli earned a BA in History from UCLA and an MA in Broadcast Journalism from San Francisco State University. She is equally grateful to have reported from both Hollywood red carpets and the comfort of her Bay Area home.

#5441. ‘We Got an Abandoned Mobile Home for Free–and Spent $14K Transforming It’

An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.

But getting the home for free was only the beginning. What followed was months of demolition, electrical and plumbing work, drywall installation, and a race to get the aging property ready for its new owner.

Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.

“I don't think I've ever had an opportunity like this before in my life, and so to turn it down would have been a shame,” Betty tells Realtor.com®. “And I know I would have regretted it, so this was probably one of the better decisions I've made in my life.”

The family spent approximately $14,000 transforming the 1977 mobile home—a fraction of what Betty spent on rent in a year. Betty finally moved in the first week of May 2026, and now, just six months later, she is hosting her first Thanksgiving in the home her family helped bring back to life.

Lyman has worked in rental property maintenance and renovation since 2001, so he knew about the home in his small town of Irrigon, OR, that had been abandoned by the owner about five years earlier.

He discussed taking over the mobile home to renovate it and rent it out to someone in need. The landlord would be able to transfer the title to Lyman and later collect rent on the lot. Meanwhile, Lyman would be able to remove the property from the landlord’s possession.

“It was kind of like a ‘I scratch your back, you scratch my back’ kind of deal,” Branson tells Realtor.com.

Initially, Lyman saw the renovation as another project for his YouTube channel, which he launched in early 2025. But the timing was also opportune for his sister, whose living circumstances had unexpectedly changed just days before he called.

Betty had been searching for another rental and considered buying an RV, paying approximately $800 a month for space at an RV park. Instead, her brother presented her with an opportunity to finally own a place of her own.

Betty could contribute what her brother calls “sweat equity,” working on the property before and after her regular job.

The purchase price was zero, but the property was far from move-in ready. The floors and walls were rotted, and there were leaks, water damage, and missing sections of ceiling.

“Basically, it was ready for the dump,” Lyman says.

With more than two decades of experience in the industry, he recognized that the structure was salvageable and the renovation worthwhile. Betty, however, was less convinced.

“I was a little overwhelmed and kind of scared when I first saw it,” she recalls.

She saw the home's many problems, including the broken countertop and the hole in the wall where a window would later be installed.

The home remained in its original location, eliminating the expense of transporting it. However, it was still sitting on flat tires and had never been properly set up. So the family's first task was to stabilize the structure on blocks.

The landlord waived the lot rent for six months while the family obtained the necessary permits. Renovation began in October 2025. Lyman and his father, with help from other family members, updated the almost 50-year-old mobile home to current building codes.

They replaced broken flooring, added insulation and drywall, and wrapped the outside of the home to protect it from the elements. Lyman shared the process on his YouTube channel.

Walls were painted, the bathroom drywall was finished, and the overall interior was beginning to look like a home. But the project wasn't without setbacks.

“There were a couple times that I was still in the middle of it all, and I'm like, 'We're too far in. I can't quit now,'” Betty recalls. “But this is hard and this is scary.”

She had to depend on her brother and her father for help when various issues arose during the renovation.

“I'm so grateful because without them, this wouldn't have been possible for me,”  she says.

Betty received her certificate of occupancy two weeks before the permit expired.

“I was actually really amazed that we were able to make it in the time frame that we did with how much that was done,” she says.

The renovation offered Betty something she had never experienced in 20 years of renting. She got to design the layout of her living space. She got to pick out the locations of her light switches and outlets. Her daughters, who share a bedroom, chose paint colors and the arrangement for the closets.

“It was an experience for me that I'll never forget,” Betty says.

The renovation of the free mobile home came with substantial expenses.

LeAnna Branson, Lyman and Betty's mother, who kept track of the receipts for the renovation, tells Realtor.com that the family initially budgeted between $10,000 and $12,000. However, rising material costs, unexpected damage discovered during demolition, and decisions to upgrade certain features pushed the total to approximately $14,000.

Betty also opted to spend a little more on higher-quality materials and finishes, knowing she intended to live there for years.

“I could have gone cheaper. Definitely, we could have cut some costs here and there,” she says. “But I plan to be here for a while. I want it to last.”

Betty used her savings to kick-start the renovation and lived in her sister’s RV, which allowed her to devote her income to the renovation for six months. Once she moved in and began paying rent on the lot, plus utilities, the pace of the work slowed a bit.

Now, Lyman estimates the renovation is approximately 90% complete. The remaining work involves the upper kitchen cabinets, wall tile, a window replacement, and several finishing touches.

The family also received support from viewers of Lyman's YouTube channel, who contributed an estimated $1,000 to $2,000. Even the handles that will adorn Betty's kitchen cabinets and drawers were paid for by a viewer.

“More support than I ever imagined,” Lyman says of the response to the project. His viewers “loved seeing the family aspect.”

For Betty, the financial benefits extend well beyond the renovation costs. She says she has more living space than she would have gotten in an apartment. And there's space for her daughters and her dog.

“We went over budget a little, but considering [Betty] was paying $20,000 a year to rent, $14,000 is not that bad,” LeAnna says. “I mean it's a chunk of money, but it's doable.”

Lyman believes owning a mobile home, even when you must rent the land it sits on, can offer an affordable housing alternative to people struggling to keep up with rising rental costs across the country.

“That was important for Betty as well, so that she could afford to live the life she deserves,” he says.

Though Betty’s experience shows that acquiring a free or inexpensive mobile home is only a small part of the financial equation, her brother’s professional experience, the family’s help, and the landlord’s willingness to waive her lot rent during the renovation also helped keep costs manageable.

For her parents, seeing their daughter choose everything from her kitchen sink to her bathroom tile was particularly rewarding.

“It gave us a peace of mind to know, you know, that she finally has a place of her own to call her home,” her mother says.

Some of the most special features of her new home are things visitors won’t see. Behind her new cupboards are messages from her family who helped her renovate her home.

“I have places on the wall behind some of the cupboards where the family all, like, signed their names and left me love notes,” Betty says. “I know they're there, even though some of them are covered up.”

The transformation is a daily reminder of what her family made possible.

“The fact that it was my family that assisted me along the way makes it even more special,” she says. “It wasn't just hiring outside help, but family and friends that came to put in the time and effort that they could to help. It makes it mean so much more to me.”

Andrea Cavallier is a New York City-based journalist and contributor to Realtor.com News, specializing in crime and investigative reporting. She previously worked as a senior crime reporter at The Independent and a digital producer for NBC’s Dateline, where she covered some of the nation’s most high-profile criminal cases. A North Carolina native, she graduated from the University of North Carolina Wilmington with a bachelor’s degree in journalism.
