#5440. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:

#5439. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5438. Why the Northeast Could Lead a Factory-Built Housing Boom

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional new construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

For one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

For years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these new chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this new category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

Realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this new type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

Six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built new construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

In third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but new-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built new construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

While the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s new manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5437. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

BTC price faces another potential sell-off as it awaits today’s inflation report after weeks of heavy selling. Core PCE is expected to rise 0.3% month over month, while 21Shares puts Bitcoin’s realized price at $53,250. A hotter reading could bring that level closer than we want.

The Binance hack initially sent Bitcoin lower, but the price recovered most of its losses by November 4. The sell-off picked up again afterward, driven by ETF withdrawals, shrinking stablecoin balances, and traders being forced out of leveraged positions.

Core PCE is forecast to rise 0.3% month over month, with annual inflation expected at 3.2%. The figure matters as markets reassess the outlook for interest rates and how much room the Federal Reserve has to ease policy.

🇺🇸8:30 AM ET COULD GET EXPENSIVE FOR OVERLEVERAGED TRADERS.September PCE: 3.6%October forecast: 3.8%Core PCE: 3.1% → 3.2% expected.The Fed wants 2%, but inflation is still sitting significantly above that target.If today’s numbers surprise lower, risk assets could… pic.twitter.com/TNuSlaiwx6

Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp reversal this month. The latest drop followed a brief Nvidia-tied recovery that brought BTC back above $60,000, but momentum quickly faded. A hotter inflation reading could put that recovery further out of reach, as Bitcoin is currently struggling to attract sustained buying.

A softer report could help prices recover, but markets are looking for more than a single green candle after several failed attempts to reverse the decline.

Bitcoin Hyper is down to its final day before launch, and the presale price is still low at just $0.0136. That’s the price buyers can get today, with tomorrow’s launch bringing the presale to a close and exchange trading expected to follow.

The timing is what makes this interesting. Tomorrow, the presale price disappears. Anyone planning to buy after launch will have to enter through the market, where the price could move either way. If demand carries over from the presale, waiting could cost buyers a cheaper entry.

$0.0136 is the presale price today, not tomorrow. With $33.2 million raised and launch just around the corner, anyone still considering HYPER is running out of time.

21Shares puts Bitcoin’s realized price at $53,250, based on Glassnode data from November 22. The figure tracks the average value of Bitcoin based on the price at which coins last moved on-chain.

Bitcoin falling toward that level would put more holders underwater. The firm also outlined a deeper scenario near $43,800, a potential 18% drop below realized price. It considers that outcome less likely, given the institutional presence and spot Bitcoin ETFs that were missing during earlier bear markets.

The report also points to fading demand and forced liquidations as major contributors to BTC price decline. The Binance hack may have triggered the initial selloff, but 21Shares argues that the subsequent weakness was driven by deteriorating market demand.

Bitcoin now needs to reclaim $60,000 and hold it. Otherwise, $53,250 could become the next level as the market searches for a floor.

#5435. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5433. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

#5431. Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

Identity security company 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the company, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company says, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the company claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Users with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the company said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will update its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

#5430. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5428. Thanksgiving Murder Mystery Remains Unsolved 30 Years After Killer Allegedly Used Cat Door to Enter Woman’s Texas Apartment

For 30 years, Thanksgiving has been a painful reminder for a Texas family whose holiday turned into a nightmare when their loved one was found strangled inside her Houston apartment.

Kristen Lea Wilson, 29, was preparing to spend Thanksgiving with her family in November 1996 when investigators say someone slipped into her first-floor apartment through a window, using a cat door to gain access, and waited for her to return home.

After cutting the telephone cord and unscrewing the lightbulbs to keep the apartment dark, the intruder waited in Wilson’s bedroom closet.

When she never showed up to Thanksgiving dinner the following day, her parents became worried and drove her apartment where they found her slain body. Three decades later, no one has been charged in her murder, and her family is still fighting for answers.

“Thirty years ago this Thanksgiving my sister Kristen Lea Wilson was murdered in Houston,” Kelly Wilson Hancock wrote in a recent social media post. “She was strangled–this was an up and personal murder. Her case has NEVER been solved.”

On Nov. 27, 1996, the day before Thanksgiving, Wilson stopped at a grocery store after work to pick up last-minute items for the family's holiday gathering at her grandparents' home in Katy, TX.

She returned to her apartment on Meadowglen Lane in southwest Houston, unloaded her groceries, and reportedly went into her bedroom to change clothes. Investigators believe her killer was already inside.

According to the Houston Police Department, the intruder likely gained access by reaching through a cat door in the screen of a first-floor window and removing the window frame. Once inside, the killer allegedly cut the telephone cord and unscrewed lightbulbs, reportedly preparing to ambush Wilson in complete darkness.

The apartment's accessibility became a crucial detail in the investigation, and raised troubling questions about security at the complex, especially because Wilson had allegedly expressed concerns about her safety before her death, her family said. She had previously revealed an incident in which a maintenance worker allegedly entered her apartment without warning.

When Wilson’s parents arrived at her apartment to check on her, they found the front door unlocked. Inside, Wilson's father made the horrific discovery–his daughter dead on the bedroom floor. She had been strangled and was partially undressed.

Police also noted a disturbing detail–her body appeared to have been deliberately positioned, with her ankles crossed and her hands resting in her lap.

Investigators found evidence of a violent struggle, including broken fingernails, suggesting Wilson had fought desperately against her attacker. There were no reported witnesses to the killing, and surveillance cameras did not capture the suspect leaving the property.

Despite decades of investigation, extensive media coverage and advancements in forensic technologies, the identity of Wilson’s killer remains a mystery.

Three men associated with Wilson provided DNA samples to investigators shortly after her death, and each were ruled out as suspects based on the technology available at the time, according to an investigation by ABC13 Houston.

But Hancock believes mistakes made during the initial investigation have complicated efforts to solve her sister's murder.

“From the get go, the detectives messed up,” she wrote in her recent post. “The original detective was going through a divorce and she wasn’t focused.”

She also expressed frustration over what she described as inconsistencies in the investigation. Investigators have since discovered that not all the evidence collected from the crime scene was tested, according to local reports.

Hancock said she has attempted to contact Othram, a forensic DNA laboratory that specializes in helping law enforcement investigate cold cases, about potentially examining evidence in her sister's murder.

“I’ve tried to reach out to Othram Labs to see if they can look at DNA, but the detective has to request it, from what I am told,” she wrote.

It is unclear whether Houston police have submitted evidence for additional testing or whether forensic genetic genealogy could be used in the case.

For the Wilson family, Thanksgiving had always been one of their favorite celebrations.

“Thanksgiving was the biggest event of the year,” Hancock told ABC13. “We’d all go over there, and it was just a big family get-together. It was so much fun.”

Wilson, described by her sister as independent and ambitious, had launched a small business that provided office services to local companies. Wilson, the middle of three girls, was also devoted to her family, especially her young niece and nephew.

"She was like a second mother to my son and daughter,” Hancock said. “She was just so beautiful with an infectious smile. My mom always called her the golden child because she just was. I hate to say she was perfect, but she pretty much was.”.

The Wilson family was devastated by her murder and to this day are still struggling with questions that remain unanswered three decades later.

“My grandma used the words ‘brutally murdered.’ I’ll never forget the call telling me Kristen had been killed," Hancock said. "My whole world was… our whole family’s world was turned upside down. Personally, I think she knew the person, but I don’t know."

Wilson's father, who discovered her body, has since passed away without learning who killed his daughter.

As the family marks the 30th anniversary of Wilson's death this Thanksgiving, her sister continues to push for answers.

Hancock said Houston police Detective Richard Rodriguez, who previously discussed the case in ABC13's Unsolved series, is now handling the investigation. She is hoping that with fresh eyes on the case, renewed publicity and advances in forensic technology might finally produce a breakthrough.

But no matter how much time has passed, Wilson's sister said the anniversary is another reminder of the holidays, birthdays and other family events her sister has missed.

“Hug your loved ones tight, you just never know," she wrote. "Miss my sister so much."

Anyone with information about Wilson's murder is urged to contact the Houston Police Department or Crime Stoppers of Houston.

#5427. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space

Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”

Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”

According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

#5426. Yearly Inflation Measures Still Hot; Economics Professor Deems December Rate Hike ‘A Done Deal’

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, released monthly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), showed an increase of 0.3% in October. The PCE price index gained 0.5% in September, making October a very slight cooldown.

The “core” PCE price index, or the PCE price index with food and energy data excluded, held steady at a 0.3% month-to-month increase.

The PCE price index is widely considered to be the Fed’s favored measure of inflation, and thus a cooldown in PCE price index gains may also signal a cooldown in Fed rate hikes.

The year-to-year data, however, point in the opposite direction. Compared to October of last year, the PCE price index actually increased 3.8%, a 0.2% gain from the same year-to-year comparison in October.

The Core PCE price index also shot up 3.3% compared to October of last year. Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long called this “(a)nother hot inflation reading” on X and remarked that “Core came in hotter than expected. It’s yet another reminder that the inflation problem right now goes beyond a mere energy shock.”

University of Pennsylvania Economics Professor Mohamed A. El-Erian made the implications of the PCE report very clear in a post on X: “All this will leave markets feeling that a Fed rate hike on December 9th is essentially a done deal, disappointing those who were hoping for a quick repeat of 2018.”

A Fed rate hike in December is likely disheartening news for the housing market, which has already seen a “crater(ing)” of pending home sales due to a high October spike in mortgage rates.

Rates have already edged down (and back up again, albeit remaining lower than the highest of the October highs), but anticipation of a rate hike may not grant buyers the confidence needed to reenter the market.

In other news, though, the latest BEA report also recorded a current-dollar PCE rise of 0.3% in October, the equivalent of $63.8 billion. The increase in expenditures is downstream of increased spending on goods and services, in which the BEA’s category of “other nondurable goods” represented the highest increase. Motor vehicles and parts experienced the largest decrease.

Lastly, personal income increased $201.8 billion or 0.7% month-over-month. According to the report, this increase mostly reflected increases in compensation, government social benefits and personal income receipts on assets.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5425. U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October

U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”

There’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

This report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

#5424. How the Kennedys Spent Thanksgiving at Their Hyannis Port Compound—Where JFK and His Father Plotted a Presidential Run

When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house.

Joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

Five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father.

He had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one.

By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to plan.

The house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose, brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9.

According to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family.

John eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property.

Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Big House.

In "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating plan. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table.

Everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird.

“They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she said.

The weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start.

Dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table.

By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children.

One family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice.

Back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies.

Ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner.

Ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped.

“For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times.

A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from.

#5422. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5421. US intelligence agencies reportedly brief Congress about Alice Huang

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

The classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is said to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The company is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

On Oct. 29, the Times revealed that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

According to the Times, this week’s classified Congressional briefing included a summary of the information that U.S. intelligence agencies have collected about Alice Huang. Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are said to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

The briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

On Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

The briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.
